name: Don't over-pluck / regrow

lead: This is the grooming advice to stop tweezing so thin or gappy brow areas can fill in, giving fuller-looking brows over time. Tweezing is the most common way to shape brows.

Plucking pulls the hair from the follicle. Where follicles are not scarred, hair may regrow once the pulling stops; where they are scarred, loss can be permanent. No clinical studies specific to over-plucking were found.

paras: People put the tweezers down for a period, often several weeks to months, and fill gaps with pencil or powder in the meantime. Some limit shaping to trimming or clean-up of stray hairs only.

Persistent pulling can cause permanent hair loss, and over-tweezed brows are a recognized reason for transplant surgery. Brow loss can also signal an underlying condition, so persistent thinning is worth raising with a clinician.

web.title: 5 ways to get overplucked eyebrows to grow back (Cleveland Clinic)

angle.text: Stopping tweezing lets sparse brow areas fill in so brows look fuller over time. It works by letting dormant follicles resume growth, which depends on whether the follicles are still intact. No trials test it.

lead: "Don't over-pluck" is grooming advice, common in looksmaxxing and beauty circles, to cut back on tweezing, waxing and threading so that thin or patchy eyebrows can fill in. Fuller, more even brows frame the eyes and are widely treated as part of a more balanced face, so people who have over-tweezed often pause plucking to recover density.[1]

Tweezing is the most common way to shape brows, and men in Western societies have increasingly plucked parts of theirs.[1] Cleveland Clinic dermatologist Shilpi Khetarpal says most brows grow back within a few months, with new growth taking at least two to three months to appear, though daily plucking can scar follicles so that hairs in them may not return.[2]

How much comes back depends on whether the follicle is intact. Hair loss from brows and lashes (madarosis) may regrow when non-scarring causes are removed, while scarring loss is permanent and is treated cosmetically, for example by transplantation.[3] Wikipedia notes that people who have over-tweezed are considered candidates for eyebrow transplants, and that constant pulling of lashes can cause permanent damage.[1][4]
infobox: Roughly two to four months for new growth to appear, per one dermatologist[2]
Topical minoxidil, eyebrow transplant, prostaglandin analogs for lashes

paras: Tweezing, waxing and threading remove brow hairs from the follicle, and the shape people favour has changed repeatedly over the decades. Proponents of leaving brows alone say that frequent removal thins them over time and that stopping lets them recover.[1] Some also say that growing the brows out for several weeks shows what the natural shape and density are before any shaping resumes.

Khetarpal told Cleveland Clinic that the brow growth cycle runs about three to four months, that most brows come back within a few months, and that plucking every day can cause damage and possibly scarring.[2] She recommends limiting plucking, waxing and shaving while brows recover, and describes over-the-counter minoxidil as something that can stimulate brow hair, with the caution that it can irritate the eyes and grow hair elsewhere on the face.[2] She lists eyebrow transplant as an option to discuss with a dermatologist if nothing grows after about four months.[2]

Lashes pulled out take about seven to eight weeks to grow back, according to Wikipedia, and constant pulling may cause permanent damage.[4] Madarosis has many causes, including blepharitis, skin conditions, nutritional deficiency, and hair-pulling disorders such as trichotillomania. Its regrowth depends on whether follicles are scarred.[3] Sudden or severe brow thinning can also have medical causes, which clinicians assess separately.[3]
No studies found. No published trial has tested stopping tweezing as an intervention for brow density; the figures above come from clinician commentary and general references on hair loss.[3][2]
